elements.name: Traceability
elements.documentation: The ability to track a product’s journey from origin to end-user – is crucial for non-profit and Public Health work. Whether distributing medicines, food aid, or other essential goods, organizations need end-to-end visibility to ensure products are authentic, safely handled, and actually reach intended beneficiaries. By assigning unique identifiers to products and capturing their movements in a digital system, stakeholders can quickly pinpoint where an item is at any given time or isolate issues (like a bad batch of medication) and initiate targeted recalls[1]. In low-resource settings, improving traceability boosts trust and reduces fraud, theft, and counterfeiting – common problems that undermine humanitarian efforts[2][3]. Overall, robust traceability systems enhance transparency and accountability, which are core values in Public Health supply chains.

elements.name: Capability (MS)
elements.documentation:
A high-level ability that an organization, system, or individual possesses or must develop in order to achieve its strategic goals. It expresses what the enterprise is able to do, independent of how that ability is implemented.



A capability is usually named using a phrase that emphasizes “what we do”. It represents an outcome-oriented, strategic abstraction of the enterprise’s abilities. 

Examples: 
- Patient Registration & Intake
- Medication Prescribing & Dispensing
- Clinical Decision Support

elements.name: Product
elements.documentation:
The concrete offering, which is made available to stakeholders. 

It bundles together services, data, and rules into a package that delivers value. Products make capabilities consumable by users. 

For example, the Trusted Personal Health Record or the National Surveillance Dashboard are products delivered in the DPI-H context.



A product represents a coherent collection of services and/or passive structure elements, accompanied by a contract, which is offered as a whole to (internal or external) customers. 



This definition covers both intangible, services-based, or information products that are common in information-intensive organizations, as well as tangible, physical products. A financial or information product consists of a collection of services along with a contract that specifies the characteristics, rights, and requirements associated with the product. “Buying” a product gives the customer the right to use the associated services. Generally, the product element is used to specify a product type. The number of product types in an organization is typically relatively stable compared to the processes that realize or support the products. “Buying” is usually one of the services associated with a product which results in a new instance of that product (belonging to a specific customer). Similarly, there may be services to modify or destroy a product. A product may aggregate or compose business services, application services, technology services, business objects, data objects, and technology passive structure elements (artifacts and material), as well as a contract. Hence a product may aggregate or compose elements from other layers than the Business Layer. A value may be associated with a product. The name of a product is usually the name used in the communication with customers, or possibly a more generic noun (e.g., “travel insurance”).

elements.name: Warehouse Management System
elements.documentation: The capabilities necessary to managing the flow of stock into the facility, its current disposition, and the flow of stock out of the facility.

elements.name: Order Management System
elements.documentation: Manage the process of capturing, approving, allocating and tracking the requests against inventory.

elements.name: Procurement Management System
elements.documentation: Managing the creation, processing, and invoicing of the purchase orders and the visibility into the fulfillment progress.

elements.name: Forecasting & Supply Planning System
elements.documentation: Capture and analyze data on demand, inventory levels, open purchase orders, and pending replenishments to forecast and plan future needs, across programs and levels of care. Demand Planning involves forecasting future requirements based on historical patterns and anticipated future conditions. Supply Planning applies constraints including funding availability, procurement mechanisms, stock-on-hand, and lead times to develop executable plans that meet those needs.

elements.name: Transportation Management System
elements.documentation: Managing the process of route management, transportation execution, freight audit and payment.

elements.name: Dispensing System
elements.documentation: The ability to record the act of preparing and giving stock to a patient or consumer. This includes the list of minimums that any system providing direct distribution of medical goods should be able to provide for.

elements.name: Analytics & Reporting Platform
elements.documentation: The ability to track key performance indicators, produce standard reports and allow for custom report development and analytics on the data. All threshold KPIs should be configurable by the administrator of the system.

elements.name: Product Catalog Management System
elements.documentation: The process of managing key master data required to effectively support the systems in use and interoperate with the larger technology ecosystem. This product master data must be aligned with national essential medicines list and has information on category/classification, route of administration, dosage form and strength with a method to keep the product list current.

elements.name: Health Facility Logistics Management System
elements.documentation: The capabilities necessary to managing the flow of stock into the health facility, its current disposition, and the flow of stock out of the facility. In this case, outbound processing describes when a facility is also acting as a local redistribution hub that is able to share or move stock to other facilities.

elements.name: Supplier & Contract Management System
elements.documentation: Managing sourcing and contracting strategies, handling tender management, and tracking supplier performance.

elements.name: Asset Management / CCE System
elements.documentation: The process of managing the key assets that handle cold chain equipment.

elements.name: CDE-HWR: Core Data Elements for the Health Workforce Registry
elements.documentation:
CDE-HWR: the Core Data Elements of the Health Workforce Registry. The deliberately minimal record the HWR holds as the system of record for each health worker:
1. Named demographics (name, sex, date of birth).
2. Identifier and index: the national unique health worker identifier, with cross-references to foundational ID where the law allows.
3. Licensure: licence number, issuing body, status, validity dates.
4. Registration: professional registration and cadre (ISCO-08 based health worker classification).
5. Educational credential: qualification, awarding institution, year.
6. Organizational affiliation: employer or other affiliating organization.
7. Facility association: the facility or facilities where the worker practises, by Facility Registry identifier.
Anything else (employment transactions, payroll, training history, etc.) stays in the operational system that owns it.

elements.name: NHWA Dataset (linking and indexing, built on CDE-HWR)
elements.documentation: National Health Workforce Accounts (NHWA) dataset. Not a second registry: an analytical linking and indexing dataset that builds on CDE-HWR. The HWR identifier is the key that links records about the same worker held in other data systems, which the NHWA handbook lists as potential data sources: the health workforce registry or database, facility administrative records and HMIS, professional council registers, labour force surveys and population census. From these, the 29 NHWA indicators in 4 modules are computed (1 stock and flow; 2 education; 3 finance and expenditures; 4 working conditions, governance and leadership) and reported nationally and to the WHO NHWA platform. Source: WHO, National health workforce accounts: a handbook, 2nd ed., 2023 (ISBN 9789240081291): the NHWA is "a system by which countries progressively improve the availability, quality, and use of data on health workforce through monitoring of a set of indicators", using diverse existing data sources (core principles: multi-sectoral governance, progressive implementation, no primary data collection).

elements.documentation:
The deployed IT system that provides the functionality. 



Components encapsulate logic and data, and expose their behavior through services. They are modular, replaceable, and reusable. 



For example, the Client Registry, Interoperability Middleware, or Terminology Serviceer are application components within DPI-H.

elements.name: Application Service (MS)
elements.documentation:
An explicitly defined application behavior. An application service exposes the functionality of components to their environment. 


It is the IT functionality that fulfills the business outcome. Application services are expressed as useful units of behavior. They link business capabilities to the application that enables them.

For example, “Consent Management Service” or “FHIR API Service”. 

This functionality is accessed through one or more application interfaces and is realized by one or more application functions that are performed by the component. It may require, use, and produce data objects. An application service should be meaningful from the point of view of the environment; it should provide a unit of behavior that is, in itself, useful to its users. It has a purpose that states this utility to the environment in terms of the value it delivers, modeled as a value element associated with the service. This means that if this environment includes business processes, application services should have business relevance. An application service may serve business, application, and technology behavior or active structure elements. An application function or process may realize an application service. An application interface may be assigned to an application service. An application service may access data objects. The name of an application service should preferably be a verb ending with “-ing”; e.g., “transaction processing”. Also, a name explicitly containing the word “service” may be used.

Goal (MS)
elements.documentation:
A high-level statement of intent, direction, or desired state for an organization and its stakeholders. 

Goals are expressed qualitatively, and can represent anything a stakeholder may desire, such as a state of affairs, or a produced value.  Goals define direction and intention, and may be broken into smaller sub-goals or linked to measurable outcomes. 

Goals are typically used to measure success of an organization and it is common to associate concrete outcomes with goals. 



Examples:

* Universal access to personal health records

* Optimize Supply Chain Management

* Enhance Climate Resilience with Predictive Capabilities

elements.name: Outcome
elements.documentation:
An end result, effect, or consequence of a certain state of affairs. 

A Business Outcome is what is actually achieved by implementing capabilities—it is the tangible, often measurable result. Outcomes are frequently tied to KPIs and may be time-bound. Outcomes can also be used to model potentially unwanted effects; for example, in order to design appropriate mitigating measures.

For example, “80% of citizens issued with a verifiable health record” or “90% of adverse events reported within 24 hours”. Outcomes demonstrate whether the architecture is delivering on its goals.

elements.name: Stakeholder
elements.documentation:
An individual, role, or organization with an interest in the outcomes of the architecture. 



Stakeholders set or influence goals and are linked to the values they expect to receive. 

Typical stakeholders in healthcare include patients and other health service users, health workers, facilities, regulators, public health agencies and international agencies.

elements.name: Value
elements.documentation:
The benefit or utility gained by a stakeholder from using a service, product, or capability.

Value captures why a goal or capability matters and who benefits. Value can be monetary, but in health contexts it often reflects non-monetary benefits such as trust, usability, or equity. 

For example, a citizen values secure access to their data, while a health worker values having a complete clinical history at the point of care.
